EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impressive long lasting period of foggy conditions prevailed across the San Joaquin Valley from January 12th through January 31st (It continued through February 7th). Dense fog coverage increased for the next several days each morning starting on the 11th. A localized area with near zero visibility was reported south of Fresno on the morning (around 9:15 AM) of the 11th that unfortunately resulted in a multi-vehicle collision that caused quite a few injuries and one fatality. Fog continued to develop each night and morning for at least another week afterward with some locations remaining foggy for the entire day during the 16th until the 19th, or only a brief improvement in visibility during the afternoon hours.||On the 20th and 21st, most locations in the Central Valley continued to observe fog during the nighttime and morning hours, but was not as widespread. Also, valley fog onset was largely later in the evening on the 20th. The fog pattern continued through the end of the month, except most locations in the San Joaquin Valley did not observe dense fog on the night of the 27th into the morning of the 28th due to an upper-level disturbance (with the exception of Merced). The fog continued through the end of the month. However, more major accidents due to fog happened on the 27th and 31st with numerous injuries reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: ASOS station KHJO Hanford Airport reported 0.25 mile visibility.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High astronomical tides combined with storm surge based off westerly swell and strong winds contributed to major coastal flooding impacts during the first few days of January. Impacts were seen across the coastal regions of the Bay Area and Central Coast, including locations of the Pacific coast that were typically insulated from the impacts of tidal flooding. A Coastal Flood Advisory was put in place starting December 31 through January 5, initially for the San Francisco and Monterey Bays but eventually including the Pacific Coast. A Coastal Flood Warning was put in place for January 2 and 3 for the San Francisco and San Pablo Bayshore areas. The San Francisco tide gauge reached 8.40 feet above MLLW on January 3, which would make it the fourth highest water level at the station on record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roadway flooding was reported on the Seminary onramp to southbound US Highway 101.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A series of storms impacted the Bay Area and Central Coast from January 1st to the 5th, causing numerous flooding impacts and scattered thunderstorms. A low pressure system on the 1st was followed by a strong cold front and associated atmospheric river late on the 2nd into the morning of the 3rd.  A second cold front followed on the 4th. A tornado warning was issued on January 5 for the Pacific coast near the border between San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties due to a radar indicated rotation signature. Around 3,400 customers in San Francisco lost power on the 2nd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The PG&E station at Pine Mountain Fire Road reported a gust of 71 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High astronomical tides combined with storm surge based off westerly swell and strong winds contributed to major coastal flooding impacts during the first few days of January. Impacts were seen across the coastal regions of the Bay Area and Central Coast, including locations of the Pacific coast that were typically insulated from the impacts of tidal flooding. A Coastal Flood Advisory was put in place starting December 31 through January 5, initially for the San Francisco and Monterey Bays but eventually including the Pacific Coast. A Coastal Flood Warning was put in place for January 2 and 3 for the San Francisco and San Pablo Bayshore areas. The San Francisco tide gauge reached 8.40 feet above MLLW on January 3, which would make it the fourth highest water level at the station on record.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Eastbound lane of Tiburon Boulevard blocked with water at Blackfield Drive.

Gusty southerly winds of 35 to 50 mph were also observed at times.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol reported roadway flooding at River Road and Ord Ferry Road from heavy rain.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An impressive long lasting period of foggy conditions prevailed across the San Joaquin Valley from January 12th through January 31st (It continued through February 7th). Dense fog coverage increased for the next several days each morning starting on the 11th. A localized area with near zero visibility was reported south of Fresno on the morning (around 9:15 AM) of the 11th that unfortunately resulted in a multi-vehicle collision that caused quite a few injuries and one fatality. Fog continued to develop each night and morning for at least another week afterward with some locations remaining foggy for the entire day during the 16th until the 19th, or only a brief improvement in visibility during the afternoon hours. ||On the 20th and 21st, most locations in the Central Valley continued to observe fog during the nighttime and morning hours, but was not as widespread. Also, valley fog onset was largely later in the evening on the 20th. The fog pattern continued through the end of the month, except most locations in the San Joaquin Valley did not observe dense fog on the night of the 27th into the morning of the 28th due to an upper-level disturbance (with the exception of Merced). The fog continued through the end of the month. However, more major accidents due to fog happened on the 27th and 31st with numerous injuries reported.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: AWOS station KFCH Fresno Chandler Executive Airport reported less than one quarter-mile visibility.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system passed through the area brought windy conditions, with gusts as high as 40 mph in the Valley and above 60 mph in the Mountains. As the longwave trough continued east, a shortwave trough along its west side evolved into a cutoff low over Baja California, where it stalled. As a result, the prevailing flow over the area shifted to the northeast, leading to a Mono wind event over the southern Sierra Nevada Mountains and high winds over the Tehachapi Mountains, Mojave Slopes, and Mojave Desert, including downslope acceleration and drying in these areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level Ridge was in place across Central California from March 17th through the end of the month. As a result, well above average temperatures with record high temperatures were observed across the San Joaquin Valley during the period. The first 90s of the year popped up on March 17th with some daily record high temperatures being broken. ||However, the 18th brought monthly record high temperatures being tied or exceeded for most of the region, while similar highs occurred until the 21st. The above average temperatures continued through the 29th, although high temperatures were not quite as warm after the 22nd. Highs rose to the mid to upper 80s from the 23rd until the 29th in the warmest locations. Above average temperatures also persisted on the 30th, but were not quite as warm as during recent days.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Record high maximum temperature of 95 degrees set, which broke the record of 92 degrees previously set for the date in 2004. It also broke the monthly record of 94 degrees previously set in 1916 and 2004. Record high minimum temperature of 59 degrees set, which broke the old record of 58 degrees last set for the date in 2004.

First responders received reports of the overturned kayak around 6 PM and multiple rescue crews from the Marin and Sonoma County Sheriff's Offices, Marin County Fire, the U.S. Coast Guard and the National Park Service responded. The woman was found unresponsive in the water, and was hoisted out of the bay and taken to shore for lifesaving measures. She was then taken to the hospital, where she was declared dead. The woman's boyfriend and a dog were located near the kayak; both survived although the boyfriend was treated for hypothermia. A nearby weather station showed winds were from the NWW that afternoon around 20-24 mph with gusts from 25-34 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A low pressure system moving through Nevada on the 19th had a strong jet on the southern side of the low. This strong jet led to strong westerly surface winds across southeastern California, with peak gusts around 40-50 mph in many locations to as high as 66 mph in the southwest corner of Imperial County. California Highway Patrol (CHP) temporarily closed a portion of Interstate 8 to high profile vehicles in southwest Imperial County the night of the 19th through early morning on the 20th. There was a CHP incident report of a semi-truck on its side and blocking one lane of I-8, with one injury, but it was unconfirmed if the cause of the accident was strong winds. Wind gusts measured by the Mountain Springs Grade RAWS station, located along I-8 near the Imperial and San Diego county border, was reaching 50-60 mph from mid afternoon on the 19th through the early morning of 20th and peaked a couple of times at 66 mph, including around the time of the reported semi-truck accident.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: California Highway Patrol (CHP) temporarily closed Interstate 8 to high profile vehicles, due to high winds, from East Willows to Ocotillo beginning around midnight and the closure lasted until around 0800PST on the 20th. Around 2230PST, CHP had an incident report about a semi-truck on its side and blocking one lane of I-8, with one injury, but the report did not confirm if the accident was due to wind. Wind gusts measured by the Mountain Springs Grade RAWS station was reaching 50-60 mph from mid afternoon on the 19th through the early morning of 20th and peaked a couple of times at 66 mph, including around the time of the reported semi-truck accident. No damages or injuries reported due to wind being unconfirmed as a cause of the semi-truck accident.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High surf conditions on February 6 resulted in two separate water rescue incidents off the coast of Santa Cruz. At 11:45 AM, surfers rescued a family of 6 from a boat that capsized off Steamer Lane. Later that day, the Coast Guard started a search at around 6:30 PM for two surfers who were seen going away from the water off the Santa Cruz Lighthouse. A High Surf Advisory was in effect for the day due to breaking waves of 17 to 22 feet. There was also a higher than normal tourist load for the region due to Super Bowl weekend activities in the San Jose and San Francisco areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A boat carrying six people, two adults and their four children, capsized off Steamer Lane near Santa Cruz around 11:45 AM on February 6. The children were wearing life vests, but the parents were not. Around ten surfers, one of whom was 14, helped to rescue the family and bring them to safety; patrol boats and ambulances arrived within minutes. The people were taken to a hospital and recovered. At the time of the incident, buoy 46236 reported swell waves of 8 ft at 16.7 seconds from the west, with wind waves of 4 ft at 9.9 seconds.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High surf conditions on February 6 resulted in two separate water rescue incidents off the coast of Santa Cruz. At 11:45 AM, surfers rescued a family of 6 from a boat that capsized off Steamer Lane. Later that day, the Coast Guard started a search at around 6:30 PM for two surfers who were seen going away from the water off the Santa Cruz Lighthouse. A High Surf Advisory was in effect for the day due to breaking waves of 17 to 22 feet. There was also a higher than normal tourist load for the region due to Super Bowl weekend activities in the San Jose and San Francisco areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Coast Guard Sector San Francisco reported that watch standers received a report around 6:30 PM on February 6 for two surfers in the water calling for help around 600 feet from the Santa Cruz Lighthouse. Coast Guard air and marine resources, Santa Cruz Fire Department and Dispatch, and Civil Air Patrol assisted in the search. The search continued until the search was suspended around 8 AM February 7. No reports of missing surfers were received by local authorities or through social media outreach, it is presumed that the two surfers were able to self-rescue. At the time of the initial report, buoy 46236 reported swell waves of 11 feet at 14.6 seconds from the west, with wind waves of 4 ft at 9.9 seconds.
